youtube_title: The Jaffa Cake Trial: Cake or Biscuit?
caption: UK VAT treats chocolate-covered biscuits and cakes differently. A tribunal weighed ingredients, texture, staling, size, packaging and more, and ruled Jaffa Cakes are cakes.
script: A British tax trial was decided by watching a snack go stale. And the snack won. [disclaimer] Meet the makers of Jaffa Cakes. A sponge base, an orange layer, and chocolate on top. In Britain, most food has no VAT. That includes cakes. Even cakes with chocolate on them. But a biscuit covered in chocolate pays the full tax. So the tax office looks at a Jaffa Cake and says, that's a chocolate biscuit. Pay up. The company takes it to a tax tribunal. And the tribunal examines a snack like a suspect. The size, the packaging, and the shop shelf all say biscuit. The name says cake, but that barely counts. The batter is eggs, flour and sugar. Like a sponge cake. Soft, not crunchy. Then the famous clue. When a Jaffa Cake goes stale, it gets hard. Like a cake. A stale biscuit goes soft. Wait. A tax trial comes down to how a snack goes stale? You see, the tribunal didn't pick one clue. It weighed all of them, like a detective with a pile of evidence. And most of it pointed to cake. Final answer. Jaffa Cakes are cakes. No VAT. Going hard was one factor, not the whole test. And this was one tax ruling, not a rule that any snack can call itself a cake. So the tax office lost a whole trial to a snack that proved itself by going stale. [loop] So before you call it a biscuit, remember

hook_old: CAKE OR BISCUIT? THE TAX TRIAL
script_old: In the U.K., this snack's tax bill depended on one question: is it a cake, or a biscuit? Here's why it mattered. In Britain, most food is zero-rated for VAT. But biscuits covered in chocolate are taxed at the standard rate, while cakes, even with chocolate on them, are not. Jaffa Cakes have a sponge base, an orange layer and a chocolate top. So the tax authority decided they were really chocolate-covered biscuits, and should be taxed. The maker, United Biscuits, took it to a VAT tribunal. And the tribunal went through the evidence like a trial. The name? Only a minor point. The ingredients? An egg, flour and sugar batter, like a sponge cake. The texture? Soft sponge, not a crisp snap. And the famous one: when a Jaffa Cake goes stale, it goes hard, like a cake. A stale biscuit goes soft. Some factors pointed the other way: the size, the packaging, and the fact that shops sell them next to biscuits. But on balance, the tribunal said: cake. So Jaffa Cakes stayed zero-rated. Going hard when stale wasn't the whole test, just one factor among many. And this is one VAT result, not a rule that any snack can call itself a cake. [loop] So before you call it a biscuit, remember
